# EHRSQL: A Practical Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Electronic Health Records

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#ehrsql)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.07695v6) · arXiv:2301.07695v6, 4 March 2026; original NeurIPS 2022 dataset paper

**Reading coverage:** All 34 pages: Sections 1–5; supplementary datasheet A, complete question/time templates B, SQL assumptions C, preprocessing D, paraphrasing E, splits F, training G, qualitative analysis H and author statement I; all tables and captions.

## Research question

Hospital staff need temporal and cohort queries beyond fixed interfaces, including requests that cannot be answered from the available EHR schema.

## Method

Turns a 222-person hospital poll into question templates, manually labels SQL for MIMIC-III/eICU, combines temporal/value slots and human/machine paraphrases, and adds held-out unanswerable requests. Processed databases shuffle patient-associated records, shift time and add synthetic costs.

## Evaluation

T5 baselines use entropy-based rejection; question templates are shared across train/validation/test while paraphrases differ. Unanswerable questions occur only in validation/test at 33%; a percentile baseline uses that prevalence explicitly.

## What the results support

Rejection improves execution precision but leaves coverage/error trade-offs. Cross-domain transfer is difficult; most EHRSQL queries cannot be parsed by the compared Spider grammar. Some ambiguous questions are folded into the unanswerable pool rather than separately resolved.

## Limits and qualifications

One-hospital question source, two databases and shared templates limit transfer claims. Temporal labels include artificial assumptions, such as diagnosis time equaling admission time in MIMIC-III. Shuffled records and synthetic costs make the dataset unsuitable for clinical inference or outcome analysis.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Core healthcare answerability benchmark with explicit temporal semantics and access requirements; benchmark precision is not evidence of clinical safety.
